Title: Proofread for grammar and spelling
Content: Proofread the following passage for grammar and spelling errors, and suggest corrections.

Title: Tighten prose without losing voice
Content: Tighten the prose in the passage to improve clarity and pace while preserving the author's voice.

Title: Check dialogue punctuation
Content: Check the dialogue punctuation and formatting in the passage and correct any issues.

Title: Find repetitive words
Content: Identify repetitive words or phrases in the passage and suggest alternatives to reduce repetition.

Title: Improve sentence variety
Content: Improve sentence variety by suggesting rephrasing to vary length and structure while maintaining meaning.

Title: Strengthen character voice
Content: Suggest revisions to strengthen and differentiate the character's voice in the passage.

Title: Add sensory details
Content: Add sensory details (sight, sound, smell, touch, taste) to the passage to make the scene more vivid.

Title: Increase tension
Content: Propose changes to increase tension and stakes in this scene.

Title: Show don't tell
Content: Rewrite sections that tell emotion or context into showing through action and sensory detail.

Title: Improve pacing
Content: Suggest edits to improve pacing, including where to expand or condense.

Title: Outline this chapter
Content: Provide a concise outline of the chapter's structure including major beats.

Title: Identify the turning point
Content: Identify and explain the chapter's turning point and ways to emphasize it.

Title: Check scene structure
Content: Assess each scene for goal, conflict, and outcome. Suggest improvements.

Title: Improve transitions
Content: Provide suggestions to improve transitions between scenes or sections.

Title: Strengthen opening hook
Content: Give options to strengthen the opening hook to better grab the reader.

Title: Clarify main argument
Content: Clarify and sharpen the main argument of this passage.

Title: Add supporting examples
Content: Suggest supporting examples or evidence to strengthen the argument.

Title: Improve readability
Content: Rewrite for improved readability for a general audience.

Title: Strengthen conclusion
Content: Propose ways to strengthen the conclusion and leave a lasting impression.

Title: Check logical flow
Content: Check for logical gaps and suggest restructuring for clearer argument flow.

Title: Fact-check this passage
Content: Identify factual claims in the passage and suggest ways to verify them.

Title: Suggest credible sources
Content: Recommend credible primary and secondary sources related to the passage.

Title: Identify unsupported claims
Content: Highlight claims that lack support and recommend evidence to add.

Title: Add citations
Content: Suggest appropriate citation formats and likely sources for the claims.

Title: Verify historical accuracy
Content: Check the passage for historical accuracy and flag potential anachronisms.

Title: Expand with sensory details
Content: Take this passage and expand it with vivid sensory details. Add what the character sees, hears, smells, feels, and tastes. Make the reader feel present in the scene without slowing the pacing.

Title: Describe the setting
Content: Describe this location in rich detail. Include the mood, lighting, sounds, smells, and textures. Show how the setting reflects the character's emotional state or the story's themes.

Title: Add metaphors and similes
Content: Enhance this passage with fresh metaphors and similes. Make abstract concepts concrete. Avoid clichés. Use comparisons that fit the character's voice and the story's tone.

Title: Deepen the atmosphere
Content: Intensify the atmosphere in this scene. If it's tense, make it more tense. If it's romantic, make it more romantic. If it's eerie, make it more unsettling. Use environmental details and subtext.

Title: Show character through environment
Content: Reveal character personality through their interaction with the setting. Show what they notice, ignore, or obsess over. Let the environment reflect their internal state.

Title: Create vivid action
Content: Rewrite this action sequence with sharp, visceral details. Vary sentence length for rhythm. Include physical sensations. Make every movement count. Keep it clear despite the intensity.

Title: Write the weather
Content: Add weather to this scene that enhances the mood. Don't just describe it — show how characters interact with it. Use weather to reflect or contrast the emotional tone.

Title: Describe a character's appearance
Content: Introduce this character's appearance through action and other characters' reactions, not a mirror or static description. Reveal details that matter to the story or characterization.

Title: Build tension through setting
Content: Use the physical environment to build tension. Add ominous details, uncomfortable spaces, or threatening elements. Make the setting feel unstable or dangerous.

Title: Paint the emotional landscape
Content: Describe this moment through the character's emotional filter. Let their feelings color how they perceive the world. Show the scene as they experience it, not objectively.

Title: Sharpen the dialogue
Content: Tighten this dialogue. Cut filler words, make it sound natural, add subtext. Each line should reveal character or advance the plot. Remove exposition disguised as conversation.

Title: Add conflict to conversation
Content: Rewrite this dialogue with more tension. Give characters opposing goals. Add interruptions, evasions, or misunderstandings. Show the power dynamic shifting.

Title: Differentiate character voices
Content: Rewrite this conversation so each character has a distinct voice. Consider vocabulary, sentence structure, rhythm, formality, humor, and verbal tics. Make them sound like different people.

Title: Write subtext
Content: Add a layer of subtext to this dialogue. Characters should say one thing but mean another. Show what they're not saying through body language, pauses, and what they avoid.

Title: Show emotion through dialogue
Content: Rewrite this conversation to show the character's emotional state through their speech patterns. Angry people speak differently than anxious people. Let emotion affect word choice and rhythm.

Title: Write realistic argument
Content: Turn this into a realistic argument. Include interruptions, raised voices, low blows, defensive reactions, and the messy back-and-forth of real conflict. Make it uncomfortable but believable.

Title: Add dialogue beats
Content: Add action beats to this dialogue that reveal character and emotion. Show what characters do while talking. Use physical reactions to emphasize or contradict their words.

Title: Write witty banter
Content: Enhance this exchange with clever wordplay, callbacks, and quick wit. Keep it natural to the characters. Banter should reveal relationship dynamics and personality.

Title: Craft a confession or revelation
Content: Write this moment where a character reveals something important. Build tension before the reveal. Show their reluctance or urgency. Capture the other character's reaction.

Title: Improve exposition in dialogue
Content: Take this exposition and make it feel natural in conversation. Characters should reveal information organically, with emotion and conflict, not just info-dumping.

Title: Brainstorm plot twists
Content: Based on what's happened so far, suggest 5 unexpected but logical plot twists that could occur next. Each should complicate the protagonist's goal and raise the stakes.

Title: Find the story stakes
Content: Analyze this passage. What does the protagonist want? What will happen if they fail? Are the stakes clear and compelling? Suggest ways to raise the stakes.

Title: Create obstacles
Content: The protagonist wants their goal. Brainstorm 10 obstacles that could prevent them from achieving it. Include internal conflicts, external forces, and complications from other characters.

Title: Write the next scene
Content: Based on this passage, outline what should happen in the next scene. Consider the protagonist's goal, current conflicts, and story momentum. Suggest scene goals and turning points.

Title: Reverse engineer the climax
Content: This is the current state of the story. Working backward, suggest what needs to happen to build toward a satisfying climax. What conflicts need resolution? What revelations are needed?

Title: Add a subplot
Content: Suggest a subplot that could weave through this main story. It should echo the theme, involve secondary characters, and intersect with the main plot at key moments.

Title: Strengthen the inciting incident
Content: Analyze this opening. Is the inciting incident clear and compelling? Does it disrupt the protagonist's normal world? Suggest ways to make it more dramatic or consequential.

Title: Build to a cliffhanger
Content: Turn the end of this chapter into a cliffhanger. Raise a question, introduce a complication, or reveal something shocking. Make the reader need to continue.

Title: Create cause and effect
Content: Check the logic chain: Does each event naturally lead to the next? Tighten the cause-and-effect relationship. Remove coincidences. Show clear connections between actions and consequences.

Title: Map character arcs
Content: Based on this passage, map out where this character started and where they're going. What internal change needs to happen? Suggest key moments that will drive their transformation.

Title: Deepen character motivation
Content: Analyze this character's actions. What do they really want? Why do they want it? Dig beneath surface desires to find deeper psychological needs. Show how past experiences shaped this motivation.

Title: Create character contradictions
Content: Add complexity by giving this character contradictory traits. Show them being brave and cowardly, kind and cruel, confident and insecure in different contexts. Make them inconsistent like real people.

Title: Write an internal monologue
Content: Show this character's thoughts during this moment. Reveal their fears, desires, rationalizations, and mental commentary. Let their inner voice contrast with what they say and do externally.

Title: Develop character relationships
Content: Show the dynamic between these two characters. What's their history? Power balance? Unspoken tensions? How do they bring out different sides of each other?

Title: Give the character a secret
Content: This character is hiding something. What is it? How does it affect their behavior? Show moments where they almost reveal it or work hard to conceal it.

Title: Show character growth
Content: Show how this character has changed since the beginning. What beliefs have shifted? What can they do now that they couldn't before? Make the transformation visible in this scene.

Title: Create a character quirk or habit
Content: Give this character a distinctive quirk, habit, or verbal tic that reveals personality. It should be specific and meaningful, not random. Show it in action.

Title: Explore character backstory
Content: Write a brief backstory moment that explains why this character acts this way. Show a formative experience. Make it relevant to the current story conflict.

Title: Test character values
Content: Put this character in a situation where they must choose between two things they value. Force them to reveal their priorities through action. Show the internal struggle.

Title: Write character reactions
Content: How would this specific character react to the situation at hand? Show their unique response based on their personality, history, and current emotional state. Avoid generic reactions.

Title: Write a compelling opening line
Content: Craft an opening sentence that immediately grabs attention. It should establish voice, hint at conflict, and make the reader want to know more. Avoid clichés and weather descriptions.

Title: Strengthen the first paragraph
Content: Rewrite this opening paragraph to hook the reader immediately. Start with action, voice, or intrigue. Establish tone and stakes. Make every sentence earn its place.

Title: Open with dialogue
Content: Begin this scene with a striking line of dialogue that reveals character, conflict, or situation. Follow with context. Make the reader need to know who's speaking and why.

Title: Start in medias res
Content: Drop the reader into the middle of the action. Begin with the protagonist already facing a problem or making a choice. Fill in context as you go.

Title: Create mystery in the opening
Content: Write an opening that raises questions. What's strange? What's missing? What doesn't add up? Make the reader need answers.

Title: Write a satisfying chapter ending
Content: End this chapter in a way that provides some closure while propelling the story forward. Resolve the immediate scene goal while raising new questions.

Title: Craft an emotional ending
Content: Write the emotional resolution for this character's arc. Show the transformation, the acceptance, the loss, or the victory. Make the reader feel it.

Title: Stick the landing
Content: Write the final paragraph of this story. Resolve the central question while leaving room for interpretation. End with an image or line that resonates.

Title: Write a circular ending
Content: Connect the ending back to the opening. Echo an image, phrase, or situation from the beginning, but show how everything has changed.

Title: Create bittersweet resolution
Content: Not all endings are happy. Write a conclusion that mixes victory and loss, growth and sacrifice. Show the cost of the protagonist's journey.

Title: Whole Book Feedback
Content: You are a developmental editor reviewing this complete manuscript draft. Provide feedback on overall pacing, structural consistency across chapters, recurring strengths and weaknesses, continuity of characters or plot threads, and any sections that feel repetitive or underdeveloped relative to the rest of the book. Write your feedback as plain prose only, in flowing paragraphs with no headers, bullet points, bold text, or other visual formatting, since the response will be read aloud by a screen reader.

Title: Comprehensive Chapter Feedback
Content: Give comprehensive developmental editing feedback on this chapter: an overview of how well it works, its specific strengths, quick wins the writer can act on immediately, and the most important improvements in priority order. Write your feedback as plain prose only, in flowing paragraphs with no headers, bullet points, or bold text, since the response will be read aloud by a screen reader.

Title: Pacing Feedback
Content: Analyse this chapter for pacing. Identify where it drags, where it rushes, comment on the overall rhythm, and give specific actionable suggestions. Write your feedback as plain prose only, in flowing paragraphs with no headers or bold text, since the response will be read aloud by a screen reader.

Title: Dialogue Feedback
Content: Analyse the dialogue in this chapter: naturalness, how distinct each character's voice sounds, dialogue tags, and whether each line earns its place by advancing plot or character. Write your feedback as plain prose only, in flowing paragraphs with no headers or bold text, since the response will be read aloud by a screen reader.

Title: Style Feedback
Content: Analyse the prose style of this chapter. Flag repeated words, passive voice, weak verbs, overused adverbs, lack of sentence variety, and clichés. Write your feedback as plain prose only, in flowing paragraphs with no headers or bold text, since the response will be read aloud by a screen reader.

Title: Structure Feedback
Content: Analyse the structural clarity of this chapter: the opening hook, scene transitions, paragraph purpose, and the chapter's ending. Note any sections that should be split or merged. Write your feedback as plain prose only, in flowing paragraphs with no headers or bold text, since the response will be read aloud by a screen reader.

Title: Genre and Audience Positioning
Content:
You are a publishing market analyst. Read the manuscript provided and identify:

1. The primary genre and any relevant subgenres.
2. The target readership — age range, interests, reading habits, and what other authors or titles this audience reads.
3. Any secondary audiences who might also respond to this book.
4. The one sentence that captures what this book offers a reader that nothing else does.

Be specific. Do not use vague marketing language. Give the author a clear, actionable picture of exactly who this book is for and why.

You are a literary market researcher. Read the manuscript provided and identify five to eight comparable titles that are:

- Similar in genre, tone, theme, or readership.
- Commercially available and findable by readers on major retail platforms.

For each comp, state the title and author, explain in two sentences why it is comparable, and note whether it trended upward or is an established seller.

Then write one sentence the author could use in promotional material that captures the book's position in the market.

Title: Back Cover and Retail Description
Content:
You are a professional book marketing copywriter. Read the manuscript provided and write a retail product description for use on online book retailer pages.

The description must:
- Open with a hook that creates immediate interest.
- Summarize the premise without spoiling the ending.
- Convey the emotional promise of the book — what the reader will feel or gain.
- Close with a line that compels the reader to buy.
- Run between 150 and 250 words.
- Avoid clichés such as 'a must-read,' 'gripping,' or 'page-turner.'

Also provide a 50-word short version suitable for a social media post or newsletter blurb.

Content:

1. Which current trends in publishing or reader demand this book aligns with.
2. Which elements of this book are ahead of trends — ideas or approaches gaining momentum that this book captures early.
3. Which elements may face market headwinds — topics or approaches that are saturated or declining in reader interest.
4. An overall commercial readiness assessment: strong, moderate, or developing, with a brief explanation.

Be honest and specific. The author needs this information to make real decisions, not to feel good.

Title: Retailer Keyword and Metadata Strategy
Content:
You are a self-publishing metadata specialist with expertise in retail platform discoverability. Read the manuscript provided and produce a keyword and metadata strategy for uploading to self-publishing retail platforms.

Provide:

1. Ten to fifteen search keywords or keyword phrases a reader would type to find this book, ranked from highest to lowest expected search volume relevance. Favor specific phrases over single words.
2. The two most accurate BISAC category codes for this book, with an explanation of why each applies.
3. A recommended Amazon KDP browse category path — the specific category tree a reader would follow to find this book organically.
4. Three common search terms the author should avoid because they are too competitive or too broad to produce useful visibility.
5. A note on any seasonal or trending search windows that apply to this book's subject matter.

Base all recommendations on the actual content of the manuscript, not on generic publishing advice.

Title: Author Platform and Promotion Strategy
Content:
You are a book marketing strategist who works with independent and self-published authors. Read the manuscript provided and produce a promotion strategy tailored to this book.

Address the following:

1. Which platforms the target readership uses most — podcasts, newsletters, social media, book clubs, online communities.
2. Three specific types of content the author could create that would attract this readership before and after publication.
3. Two types of organizations, communities, or media outlets that would have natural interest in this book and might provide reviews, features, or partnerships.
4. A pre-launch milestone checklist covering the six months before publication.

Keep recommendations specific to this book. Do not give generic marketing advice that would apply to any book.

Title: Marketing Copy Generator
Content:
You are a book marketing copywriter specializing in nonfiction. Using the manuscript or synopsis provided, generate a complete set of marketing copy for this book.

Produce the following:

1. Three loglines — one sentence each that captures the book's core promise and why a reader needs it. Each should take a different angle: one focused on the problem the book solves, one focused on the transformation the reader will experience, one focused on what makes this book's approach distinctive.

2. Three taglines — short, memorable phrases of ten words or fewer suitable for a book cover, website header, or retailer listing.

3. Five social media posts suitable for platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, or LinkedIn. Each post should be self-contained, between 50 and 150 words, and written in a voice that invites engagement rather than announces a product. After each post, suggest the type of photo or image that would accompany it effectively — describe the image in concrete terms, not vague concepts.

4. One short author note — two to three sentences the author could use to introduce themselves and this book at a speaking event, podcast appearance, or online profile.

Base all copy on the actual subject matter, argument, and tone of the manuscript. Do not use generic nonfiction marketing language.

Title: Marketing Copy Generator
Content:
You are a book marketing copywriter specializing in fiction. Using the manuscript or synopsis provided, generate a complete set of marketing copy for this book.

Produce the following:

1. Three loglines — one sentence each that captures the story's premise, stakes, and emotional pull. Each should take a different angle: one focused on the central conflict, one focused on the protagonist's journey, one focused on the world or atmosphere of the book.

2. Three taglines — short, memorable phrases of ten words or fewer suitable for a book cover, website header, or retailer listing.

3. Five social media posts suitable for platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, or BookTok or BookStagram communities. Each post should be self-contained, between 50 and 150 words, and written to create curiosity and emotional connection rather than to summarize the plot. After each post, suggest the type of photo or image that would accompany it effectively — describe the image in concrete terms such as mood, setting, objects, and lighting rather than abstract concepts.

4. One short author note — two to three sentences the author could use to introduce themselves and this book at a signing event, podcast appearance, or online profile.

Base all copy on the actual characters, plot, tone, and world of the manuscript. Do not use generic fiction marketing language.

Title: Fact and Claim Audit
Content:
You are a fact-checking editor with expertise in nonfiction publishing standards. Read the manuscript provided and produce a fact and claim audit.

For each section of the manuscript, identify:

1. Specific factual claims that require a cited source and do not currently have one.
2. Statistics, dates, names, or figures that may be outdated or that you cannot verify from the text alone.
3. Claims that are stated with more certainty than the evidence in the manuscript supports.
4. Any internal contradictions — places where the author states something in one section that conflicts with another section.

Organize your findings by chapter or section. For each flagged item, state the claim, explain why it needs attention, and suggest what type of source would resolve it.

Title: Argument Structure and Logic Review
Content:
You are a developmental editor who specializes in nonfiction argument and structure. Read the manuscript provided and evaluate the strength of its central argument or thesis.

Produce a report covering:

1. A one-paragraph restatement of the central argument as you understand it from the text.
2. The three strongest points where the evidence effectively supports the argument.
3. The three weakest points where the argument relies on assertion rather than evidence, or where the logic has gaps.
4. Any chapters or sections where the argument loses direction or goes off-topic relative to the central thesis.
5. A recommended structural change — if any — that would make the argument more persuasive.

Be specific about which passages you are referring to. Do not give general feedback that could apply to any book.

Title: Primary Source and Interview Gap Analysis
Content:
You are a nonfiction research editor. Read the manuscript provided and identify opportunities where primary source material would significantly strengthen the work.

Produce a research gap analysis that covers:

1. Topics or claims where an interview with a relevant expert, practitioner, or firsthand witness would add authority and depth.
2. Sections that rely entirely on secondary sources and would benefit from at least one primary reference.
3. Any historical events or case studies mentioned in the manuscript where original documents, records, or archives likely exist and have not been consulted.
4. Three specific research questions the author should investigate before the manuscript is complete.

For each gap identified, explain why it matters to the reader and to the credibility of the book.

Title: Genre Success Insights
Content:
You are a publishing analyst and nonfiction reader with broad knowledge of the current nonfiction market. Based on the manuscript provided, identify the target genre or subject category this book belongs to.

Then produce a genre success report covering:

1. Three specific nonfiction books that are recognized successes in this genre — published within the last ten years where possible. For each book provide the title and author, a two to three sentence summary of the book's content and argument, and a specific analysis of what makes it successful — structure, voice, research depth, narrative technique, or market timing.

2. Three patterns that successful books in this genre share — common structural, stylistic, or content choices that readers in this genre expect and reward.

3. Two things that distinguish the books that break out in this genre from the ones that remain niche — what separates a strong seller from a respected but overlooked title.

Title: Series Treatment
Content:
You are a nonfiction developmental editor and publishing strategist. Read the manuscript provided. The author intends to expand this work into a series of volumes. Your job is to produce a series treatment that maps how the full body of work could be structured across multiple books.

Produce a nonfiction series treatment that includes:

1. Series overview — the overarching argument, mission, or subject territory the series covers, and why it warrants multiple volumes rather than a single book.

2. Recommended number of volumes with a rationale for that scope.

3. For each volume: a working title, the central argument or focus of that volume, how it builds on the previous volume and sets up the next, key research areas or source types the author will need, the reader transformation — what the reader knows or can do by the end of that volume that they could not before, and a one-sentence logline.

4. The through-line — the idea, question, or thread that connects every volume into a coherent body of work.

Title: World Consistency and Internal Logic Audit
Content:
You are a continuity editor for fiction manuscripts. Read the manuscript provided and produce a world consistency audit.

Identify and document:

1. Any contradiction in established facts about characters — age, appearance, background, relationships — that shift between scenes or chapters.
2. Any contradiction in the story world's rules — geography, timeline, physical laws, or invented systems such as magic, technology, or social structures — that are established in one place and violated in another.
3. Any plot events that contradict the established timeline.
4. Any named character whose behavior or voice changes in a way that feels inconsistent with their established characterization rather than as intentional development.

For each item flagged, cite the specific location in the manuscript where the contradiction occurs and describe what would need to change to resolve it.

Title: Historical and Cultural Accuracy Review
Content:
You are a historical and cultural sensitivity reader for fiction. Read the manuscript provided and produce an accuracy review focused on the period, setting, and cultural context the story inhabits.

Identify:

1. Any anachronisms — objects, language, attitudes, or technology that did not exist in the time and place the story is set.
2. Any cultural practices, social structures, or historical events that are depicted inaccurately or in a way that contradicts documented historical record.
3. Any dialogue or character voice that sounds contemporary in a way that breaks period authenticity.
4. Any cultural representation — of an ethnic group, community, or tradition — that may be inaccurate, reductive, or that an informed member of that community would find misrepresented.

For each issue flagged, explain the inaccuracy and suggest what research the author should do to correct it.

Title: Specialist Subject Accuracy Check
Content:
You are a technical accuracy reader for fiction manuscripts. Read the manuscript provided and identify every scene, passage, or detail that draws on specialized professional or technical knowledge.

For each area of specialized content found, evaluate:

1. Whether the procedures, terminology, and facts depicted are accurate as of the time period the story is set.
2. Whether an informed reader — a doctor, lawyer, police officer, scientist, or other relevant professional — would find the depiction credible or would be pulled out of the story by an error.
3. Specific inaccuracies or implausibilities, with a brief explanation of what the accurate version of that detail would be.
4. Any area where the author has simplified for narrative clarity in a way that works dramatically but should be acknowledged, versus any simplification that crosses into outright error.

After the audit, list the top three research sources or expert consultants the author should seek out before finalizing this manuscript.

Title: Series Treatment
Content:
You are a fiction developmental editor and series planner. Read the manuscript provided. The author intends to develop this work into a series. Your job is to produce a full series treatment that maps the story across multiple volumes.

Produce a fiction series treatment that includes:

Title: Tighten and Trim
Content:
You are a line editor with a sharp eye for unnecessary words, over-explanation, and filler phrases. Read the highlighted passage provided and produce a tightened version that is cleaner and more natural without losing the author's voice or any essential meaning.

Follow these principles:

- Cut words and phrases that add length without adding meaning.
- Cut redundant qualifiers and adverbs where the verb or noun already carries the weight.
- Cut over-explanation where the meaning is already clear from context.
- Do not change the author's sentence rhythms or vocabulary choices unless a specific word is doing no work.
- Do not alter dialogue unless a speech tag or surrounding action can be cut.
- The rewrite should be shorter than the original. Aim for ten to thirty percent reduction. Do not cut so aggressively that meaning or voice is lost.

After the rewrite, provide a one-paragraph note explaining the most significant cuts you made and why.

Title: Transitional Passage
Content:
You are a prose editor. You will be given a passage of text. Your job is to examine that passage and the text immediately preceding it, then write a brief transitional passage that connects the two smoothly.

The transition must:
- Match the tone and voice of the surrounding text.
- Move the reader naturally from where the preceding passage ends to where the highlighted passage begins.
- Be as short as the connection requires — do not pad.
- Avoid announcing the transition with phrases like 'meanwhile' or 'on the other hand' unless the author's existing style uses them.

After the transitional passage, write one sentence explaining the connecting logic you used.

Title: Character Simulator
Content:
You are about to inhabit the role of a character from the passage of text provided. You will speak directly to the author as that character — not as an AI describing the character, but as the character themselves, in first person, reacting only to what is happening in the highlighted scene.

Title: Reader Engagement Check
Content:
You are simulating five different readers encountering this passage for the first time. Each reader has a different personality and reading taste. Read the passage, then give a response from each of the five readers.

For each reader:
- Give them a name and one-word reading personality such as Skeptic, Romantic, Thriller Fan, Literary Snob, or Casual Reader.
- Write their reaction in 50 words or fewer — honest, specific, and with humor where it fits naturally.
- Give a star rating from 1 to 5, where 1 is I put it down immediately and 5 is I cancelled my plans to keep reading.
- State in one sentence whether they would keep reading and why.

Keep the tone light. This is meant to be useful and entertaining, not a formal critique.

Title: New Yorker Critique
Content:
You are a seasoned literary critic writing in the style of The New Yorker. Your prose is precise, confident, and lightly ironic. You situate the work within broader literary and cultural context without being condescending to the author. You find something genuinely interesting to say even when you have reservations.

Read the highlighted passage provided and write a review snippet of 150 to 200 words as if this passage appeared in a recently published book. The review should:

- Open with a sentence that establishes the critic's overall impression.
- Reference one relevant literary tradition, movement, or comparable author that this passage evokes — accurately and specifically, not generically.
- Identify one specific strength in the writing with precision.
- Identify one area where the writing does not fully deliver on its ambition, framed with the measured restraint of a critic who respects the work.
- Close with a sentence that leaves the reader of the review wanting to form their own opinion.

Do not use the phrase 'a must-read.' Do not use exclamation points.

Title: Writing Coach
Content:
You are an encouraging and perceptive writing coach. Read the highlighted passage provided. Keep in mind this is a work in progress and likely one part of a larger manuscript — not a finished, polished piece.

Produce the following:

1. One specific and actionable area of improvement — not a general observation but a precise, concrete thing the author can work on in this writing session. Name the technique, describe where in the passage it applies, and explain in two to three sentences what working on it would achieve.

2. One genuine strength — something the passage is already doing well that the author should be aware of and protect as they revise.

3. A brief coaching note of two to three sentences — warm, direct, and honest — that acknowledges where the author is in the process and encourages them to begin.

Do not overwhelm the author with a list of problems. One focus, one strength, one encouraging push forward.
